newsitem.title: MEXICO: Split Mexico congress would hit Zedillo - report.
newsitem.headline: Split Mexico congress would hit Zedillo - report.

text.p: President Ernesto Zedillo could lose control over his party if it fails to keep its 68-year-old congressional majority in elections next month, the U.S. consulting firm Burson-Marsteller said in a report.

The report, distributed to Burson-Marsteller clients last week and obtained by Reuters Wednesday, warns of possible gridlock if the opposition steals the ruling Institutional Revolutionary party (PRI) majority in the Chamber of Deputies but it plays down the risk of chaos.

"Without a doubt, the biggest impact (of an opposition majority in the Lower House) would fall on the president. His leadership over his party would be directly affected and he would face greater problems of unity in his party as the presidential succession draws nearer," the report said.

The Burson-Marsteller report, co-written by Duke University professor Scott Morgenstern and Mexican professor Ignacio Marvan, was distributed at a Mexico City seminar last week attended by the firm's paying clients. These include Mexican businesses and multinationals with operations in the country.
About 52 million Mexicans go to the polls on July 6 to elect the lower house of Congress, a quarter of the Senate, six governors and, for the first time in modern history, a mayor of Mexico City.
Polls show Zedillo's PRI running a distant second or even third in the crucial Mexico City race, but in the congressional election the results are less clear cut.
The Burson-Marsteller report suggested the most likely scenario was that the PRI would remain the biggest single party.
But it was not clear if Zedillo's party would keep its majority in the lower house.
This is because of the country's complicated voting system, which mixes first-past-the-post races with some proportional representation.

The PRI is challenged by the conservative National Action Party (PAN) and the leftist Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD). Because only a quarter of the Senate is being renewed and the PRI has a massive majority in that chamber, its majority there is safe.

The possibility that the PRI could lose its grip in the lower house has spooked big business, because it suggests pro-market reforms sponsored by the president will no longer be rubber-stamped by a tame PRI congress.
The report said an opposition-controlled lower house could hypothetically draw up its own budget, because neither the president nor the Senate supposedly have veto powers over its budget decisions.
That would alarm many investors who fear the PAN and the PRD may be less committed to fiscal displine than the PRI.

The report also said budget negotiations were likely to be the main source of gridlock between the president and an opposition-controlled Chamber of Deputees, and that inter-party conflicts could grow as the year 2000 presidential succession approaches.
On the other hand, it noted that opposition parties would be eager to demonstrate responsibility in power, and that Zedillo was only likely to propose laws that would be widely backed in Congress.

"The possibility of conflicts -- indeed the fact that these would happen -- does not mean chaos. It means, whatever the circumstances, a learning curve for all political participants, sharing of responsibilities and the construction of a new governability," the report said.
